title: Esther 5:1–8
context: On the third day, matching the three-day fast of 4:16, Esther puts on her royal clothing and stands in the inner court facing the king on his throne (5:1). She obtains favor in his sight, and he holds out the golden scepter, which she touches (5:2), the danger of 4:11 passing without harm. The king offers her up to half the kingdom, and instead of stating her request she invites the king and Haman to a banquet she has prepared (5:3–5). At the banquet of wine the king asks again, and Esther invites them to a second banquet the next day, promising to answer then (5:6–8). The text does not explain why Esther delays, and readers suggest several reasons, such as gauging the king’s mood, building toward a fuller setting, or simple caution; this commentary leaves the reason open. The book does not name God here. Many readers in both traditions see God’s quiet providence in Esther’s favor and in the delay that sets up the sleepless night of chapter 6; that is shared ground rather than a point of division.

verses.text: Now on the third day, Esther put on her royal clothing and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, next to the king’s house. The king sat on his royal throne in the royal house, next to the entrance of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: On the third day Esther puts on her royal clothing and stands in the inner court. Arminian readers see her keeping her word from 4:16 and choosing to face the risk with dignity and careful preparation. Her courage is real and freely exercised, and the fasting of the community stands behind her action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the link between the third day and the three-day fast, and they read Esther’s appearance as faith expressed through prudent action rather than presumption. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the moment Esther acts on her resolve, note that the book does not name God even here, and avoid adding a typological meaning to “the third day” that the text does not draw out.

verses.text: When the king saw Esther the queen standing in the court, she obtained favor in his sight; and the king held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. So Esther came near and touched the top of the scepter.
verses.arminianNotes: The king sees Esther, she obtains favor in his sight, and he extends the golden scepter, which she touches. Arminian readers often see God’s gracious providence in this favorable reception, while stressing that the king’s response is genuinely his own and Esther’s courage genuinely hers. The danger of 4:11 passes without harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers frequently cite Proverbs 21:1, that the king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand, to read this favor as God’s quiet direction of the king’s will. Shared ground: both traditions see providence in Esther’s reception, both note that the book does not name God here, and both hold that God’s care works through real human responses, so seeing providence in this moment is shared ground rather than a contrast.

verses.text: Then the king asked her, “What would you like, queen Esther? What is your request? It shall be given you even to the half of the kingdom.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king asks what Esther wants and promises it even to half of the kingdom. Arminian readers take the offer as a customary expression of royal generosity rather than a literal pledge, compare Mark 6:23, and they note that it opens a door Esther must decide how to use. Her restraint in the next verses is itself a deliberate choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat “to the half of the kingdom” as a formula of generous goodwill and read the king’s openness as the favor of 5:2 taking concrete form. Shared ground: both traditions avoid reading the phrase as a literal offer, note that it will be repeated (5:6, 7:2), and see the verse as setting the stage for Esther’s careful strategy rather than an immediate request.

verses.text: Esther said, “If it seems good to the king, let the king and Haman come today to the banquet that I have prepared for him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esther invites the king and Haman to a banquet she has prepared. Arminian readers see wisdom in her approach, moving carefully rather than blurting out an accusation in open court. They note that the plan was prepared in advance, suggesting thoughtful planning alongside courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read Esther’s invitation as prudent and see wisdom as one of the ordinary means God uses. They note the irony that Haman is invited to his own undoing, though he cannot see it. Shared ground: both traditions read the banquet as strategy, note that the text does not explain why Haman is included, and avoid assigning Esther motives beyond what the story shows.

verses.text: Then the king said, “Bring Haman quickly, so that it may be done as Esther has said.” So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.
verses.arminianNotes: The king orders Haman brought quickly, and both come to Esther’s banquet. Arminian readers note the king’s eagerness to please Esther, a sign that her approach has succeeded so far. Haman’s arrival, with no knowledge of Esther’s identity, deepens the dramatic irony of the scene.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the irony that Haman hurries to a meal that will lead to his exposure, and they see providence ordering events beyond the awareness of those involved. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as building tension, and both note that banquets frame the book’s major turns (1:3, 2:18, 5:4, 7:1, 9:17–19) without forcing more meaning onto the pattern.

verses.text: The king said to Esther at the banquet of wine, “What is your petition? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.”
verses.arminianNotes: At the banquet of wine the king asks again for Esther’s petition and repeats his generous promise. Arminian readers see the king’s persistence as an open door, and they note that Esther’s timing is still hers to decide. The repeated question shows that his favor is holding steady.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the king’s renewed offer and see the repetition as heightening suspense. They read the steady favor of the king as a continuing sign of the providence that began with the scepter in 5:2. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the deliberate pacing of the story, with Esther’s request deferred to build toward the decisive moment in chapter 7.

verses.text: Then Esther answered and said, “My petition and my request is this.
verses.arminianNotes: Esther begins to answer, “My petition and my request is this.” Arminian readers see her poised on the edge of disclosure and then choosing restraint. The pause shows her weighing the moment, and many readers sense that she is still testing whether the time is right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the suspense of the half-spoken answer and read the pause as part of the wisdom that guides her approach. The narrator does not explain her hesitation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heightening suspense and avoid filling in Esther’s private reasoning, which the text leaves unstated.

verses.text: If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and I will do tomorrow as the king has said.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esther asks the king and Haman to return to a second banquet, promising to answer then. Arminian readers note that her delay is a free, considered decision whose reason is not given, and they observe that the extra day leads to events she could not have planned, as chapter 6 shows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see providence in the delay, since the intervening night brings the king’s sleeplessness and the honoring of Mordecai (6:1–11). They hold that God works through Esther’s choice without her knowing the outcome. Shared ground: both traditions see Esther’s delay as consequential, leave her motive open, and treat providence in the timing as shared ground.
